title: SHE WAS BARREN FOR 20 YEARS. THEN HER HUSBAND PRAYED—AND GOD ANSWERED WITH TWO CHILDREN WHO WOULD STRUGGLE BEFORE THEY WERE EVEN BORN.
paragraphs: SHE WAS BARREN FOR 20 YEARS. THEN HER HUSBAND PRAYED—AND GOD ANSWERED WITH TWO CHILDREN WHO WOULD STRUGGLE BEFORE THEY WERE EVEN BORN.
The untold weight of Isaac and Rebekah’s waiting, the prayer that Scripture refused to forget, and the God who was writing a greater story long before anyone could see it. — Genesis 25:21–26
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that happens when you keep praying for something that never seems to change.
You wake up. You believe again. You whisper the same prayer you whispered yesterday.
And nothing.
Another month passes. Another year disappears. Another person receives the blessing you have been begging God for.
You smile because you are genuinely happy for them.
Then you go somewhere private and cry.
Not because you hate their happiness.
But because their answered prayer reminds you of your unanswered one.
And perhaps the hardest part is not even the waiting.
It is wondering whether God has heard you at all.
Now imagine that silence lasting twenty years.
Not twenty days.
Not twenty months.
Twenty years.
That is the painful backdrop to one of the most extraordinary births recorded in Genesis.
A woman named Rebekah could not conceive.
Her husband, Isaac, was the son of Abraham—the child whose very existence testified that God could fulfill a promise beyond human expectation.
Isaac had grown up inside a miracle.
Yet when he married, he discovered that knowing God's promises did not exempt his household from painful waiting.
And here is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because sometimes the people who know the most about God's faithfulness still have to walk through seasons when His faithfulness is difficult to see.
Scripture tells us:
“And Isaac intreated the LORD for his wife, because she was barren: and the LORD was intreated of him, and Rebekah his wife conceived.” — Genesis 25:21, KJV
Read that again.
Isaac did not simply accept the situation as hopeless.
He prayed.
And the Bible makes something beautiful unmistakably clear.
He prayed for his wife.
Not against her.
Not as though her infertility made her less worthy of love.
Not because she had failed him as a woman.
He brought their suffering before the Lord.
In a world where a woman's inability to bear children could become a source of devastating social shame, this small sentence carries extraordinary tenderness.
The Scripture does not record Isaac humiliating Rebekah.
It records him interceding for her.
There is a difference between standing beside someone in their suffering and making them feel responsible for it.
And some marriages desperately need to remember that difference.
When the diagnosis comes...
When the finances collapse...
When the dream keeps getting postponed...
When the person you love is quietly falling apart...
Love does not always have the power to fix what hurts.
But love can refuse to abandon the hurting person.
Isaac's prayer was not a substitute for loving Rebekah.
It was one expression of his love.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear something they have not heard in a very long time.
Your inability to produce what others expect from you does not make you worthless.
Your value is not measured by the children you bear, the money you earn, the marriage you have, the achievements you collect, or the expectations you satisfy.
You are a human being made in God's image.
And your dignity was never supposed to depend on your productivity.
Rebekah was not less human because her womb was empty.
She was not less deserving of compassion because her longing remained unfulfilled.
And neither are you.
But there is something else in this passage that deserves our attention.
Something hidden beneath the English translation.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיֶּעְתַּר יִצְחָק לַיהוָה לְנֹכַח אִשְׁתּוֹ
Vayyeʿtar Yitsḥaq la-YHWH lenokhaḥ ishto.
“And Isaac pleaded with the LORD on behalf of his wife.”
The Hebrew verb וַיֶּעְתַּר (vayyeʿtar) comes from the root עתר (ʿ-t-r), associated with making earnest supplication.
The same Hebrew root appears again in the verse when God responds.
וַיֵּעָתֶר לוֹ יְהוָה
Vayyeʿater lo YHWH.
“And the LORD responded to his plea.”
Notice the literary beauty.
The prayer and the answer are connected through the same Hebrew root.
Isaac pleaded.
The Lord responded.
The wording draws our attention to a personal God who hears human supplication.
But we must be careful here.
The passage does not teach that repeating a prayer enough times will eventually force God to act.
It does not give us a spiritual formula for conception.
And it certainly does not mean that couples who remain childless have prayed incorrectly or lacked sufficient faith.
Genesis is telling us what God did in this particular covenant family.
It is not promising every family the same outcome.
That distinction matters.
Because careless preaching can turn somebody else's miracle into another person's wound.
And the God of Scripture does not need us to exaggerate His promises to make Him worthy of trust.
The truth is already powerful enough.
Isaac was forty years old when he married Rebekah.
Genesis 25:20 tells us that.
And Genesis 25:26 tells us that Isaac was sixty when Esau and Jacob were born.
Twenty years separated those two milestones.
The text does not tell us precisely when Isaac began praying or how frequently he prayed throughout those years.
But it does show us that the marriage endured a long season of childlessness before God granted conception.
Think about everything twenty years can contain.
Birthdays.
Anniversaries.
Family gatherings.
Quiet disappointments.
Questions nobody knows how to answer.
Perhaps hope rising again, only to be disappointed again.
We are not told every conversation Isaac and Rebekah had. We should not invent their private moments and call them Scripture.
But anyone who has waited through prolonged suffering knows that twenty years is not a small space between two Bible verses.
It is a significant portion of a human life.
And then, in the sovereign timing of God, Rebekah conceived.
But the story did not suddenly become easy.
Because sometimes an answered prayer opens the door to an entirely different kind of struggle.
Genesis 25:22 says:
“And the children struggled together within her; and she said, If it be so, why am I thus? And she went to enquire of the LORD.” — KJV
Imagine the emotional reversal.
After years of being unable to conceive, Rebekah was finally pregnant.
Yet the movement within her was so troubling that she sought an answer from God.
The Hebrew description is striking.
וַיִּתְרֹצֲצוּ הַבָּנִים בְּקִרְבָּהּ
Vayyitrotsetsu habbanim beqirbah.
“The children struggled against one another within her.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root רצץ (r-ts-ts), associated with crushing or violent pressure. In this context, it describes the intense struggle of the unborn children.
This was not merely a sentimental picture of two babies moving.
The narrator was preparing us for a conflict that would shape generations.
Rebekah had prayed through barrenness.
Now she was seeking God amid distress.
And that is a lesson many believers discover only after experiencing their own answered prayers.
Receiving what you prayed for does not mean you will never have to pray again.
The marriage you asked God for will still require grace.
The child you longed for will still need wisdom and care.
The ministry you dreamed about will still face opposition.
The opportunity you begged God to open may still demand sacrifice.
God's blessings do not eliminate our dependence on Him.
Sometimes they deepen it.
And when Rebekah sought the Lord, He answered with something far greater than a medical explanation.

“Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger.” — Genesis 25:23, KJV
Two nations.
Two peoples.
A conflict stretching beyond one household.
And a reversal of the customary expectation that the firstborn would hold precedence.
Rebekah thought she was carrying children.
She was also carrying the beginnings of a history she could not yet comprehend.
But do not miss the sobering reality.
The divine announcement was not simply a promise of uncomplicated prosperity.
It foretold division.
The children would become ancestors of peoples whose relationship would be marked by tension.
The promise of God was unfolding through a family that would know real conflict, human failure, favoritism, deception, and grief.
And still, God would not abandon His covenant purpose.
That is what makes Genesis so profoundly honest.
The Bible does not hide the brokenness of its central families.
Abraham had failures.
Isaac had weaknesses.
Rebekah would make painful decisions.
Jacob would deceive.
Esau would despise his birthright.
This family was not a polished portrait of flawless spiritual heroes.
It was a family through whom God continued working despite human sin and disorder.
And isn't that where so many of us live?
Not inside the perfect testimony.
But inside the unfinished one.
Where faith and fear exist in the same heart.
Where you love God and still have questions.
Where you have received mercy and still struggle with old habits.
Where you believe His Word but sometimes tremble at what tomorrow might bring.
Then the day of delivery arrived.
Genesis 25:24 says that Rebekah was indeed carrying twins.
The first child came out red and hairy.
He was named Esau.
Then his brother emerged with his hand holding Esau's heel.
He was named Jacob.
The Hebrew text says:
וְיָדוֹ אֹחֶזֶת בַּעֲקֵב עֵשָׂו
Veyado oḥezet baʿaqev ʿEsav.
“And his hand was holding Esau's heel.”
The Hebrew word עָקֵב (ʿaqev) means “heel” and contributes to the wordplay surrounding Jacob's name, Yaʿaqov.
Even their entrance into the world foreshadowed the rivalry that would unfold.
Two boys.
One womb.
One covenant family.
And a future filled with consequences nobody in that delivery moment could fully understand.
But here is where we must resist turning the account into a shallow motivational message.
The central meaning of this story is not simply that if you pray long enough, God will give you double.
That sounds exciting.
It makes a memorable slogan.
But it is not what Genesis 25 teaches.
The twins were not presented as a universal promise of double blessings for every person who waits.
They were two particular children within God's unfolding covenant history.
The real wonder is deeper.
God's redemptive purpose was moving forward through human weakness, prolonged waiting, and a family whose future would be anything but simple.
And that purpose ultimately leads us to Jesus Christ.
Because the story does not end with Isaac, Rebekah, Esau, and Jacob.
It continues through generations.
Through the covenant line of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Through Judah.
Through Israel's long history of rebellion, judgment, mercy, and promise.
Until, in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ came into the world.
Matthew begins his Gospel by identifying Jesus Christ as the son of David and the son of Abraham.
And in Matthew 1:2, Isaac and Jacob appear in the genealogy that leads to Christ.
The family that began with Abraham's impossible-looking promise became part of the historical line through which the Messiah came.
Not because that family was righteous enough to earn such an honor.
But because God was faithful to His covenant.
And this is where the story stops being only about a woman who could not conceive.
It becomes a window into the character of the God who saves.
The God who heard Isaac's plea is the God who would one day send His Son into a world desperate for redemption.
The God who worked through Jacob's deeply flawed family is the God who offers grace to deeply flawed sinners.
The God who did not abandon His promises amid generations of human failure is the God who fulfilled His saving purpose in Jesus Christ.
And the cross tells us something no temporary earthly blessing could ever fully communicate.
God's love is not measured by how quickly He removes our suffering.
It is revealed decisively in the sacrifice of His Son.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we fixed every mistake.
Not after we learned how to pray perfectly.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That is grace.
And it is why our theme will always be more than a beautiful phrase.
Think about Jacob.
He entered the world holding his brother's heel.
Later, his life would become entangled in deception and family conflict.
Yet God would meet him, humble him, and give him the name Israel.
His story was not the story of a flawless man who earned divine favor.
It was the story of a flawed man confronted by the faithfulness of God.
And through the history of Israel, the promised Messiah would come.
Jesus did not arrive because humanity finally became worthy.
He came because humanity desperately needed a Savior.
And perhaps that is the truth you need most tonight.
You may not be waiting for a child.
Maybe you are waiting for reconciliation with someone you love.
Maybe you are asking God to restore a marriage.
Maybe you have been fighting a private addiction and nobody knows how many times you have fallen.
Maybe you are grieving a child you never got to hold.
Maybe your prayers are not about receiving something new, but about finding the strength to survive what you have already lost.
Or maybe you have stopped praying because hope has become exhausting.
You still attend church.
You still say “Amen.”
You still tell people God is good.
But somewhere deep inside, you have begun to wonder whether His goodness includes you.
Listen carefully.
The twenty years in Isaac and Rebekah's story are not a deadline God has placed on your suffering.
Their twins are not a guarantee of your desired outcome.
And their answered prayer is not proof that every unanswered prayer is waiting for the same kind of ending.
But their story does invite you to bring your need before the Lord.
Without pretending.
Without performing.
Without treating prayer as a transaction.
You can pray while confused.
You can pray while grieving.
You can pray while trembling.
You can pray even when the only words you have left are, “Lord, help me.”
And if your circumstances do not change tomorrow, that does not mean Jesus has ceased to be your Savior.
Remember the garden of Gethsemane.
Jesus Himself prayed in deep anguish.
He asked that the cup might pass from Him, yet submitted Himself to the Father's will.
The Father did not spare Him the cross.
Through His suffering, death, and resurrection, Christ accomplished our redemption.
That is why Christian hope cannot be reduced to getting everything we ask for.
Our hope is anchored in the crucified and risen Jesus.
And His resurrection means suffering, sin, and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
So yes, pray for the miracle.
Pray for the healing.
Pray for the child.
Pray for restoration.
Pray for the breakthrough.
But above all, seek the God who is worthy of your trust even when the answer is different from what you imagined.
Because the greatest gift God offers us is not a particular earthly outcome.
It is reconciliation with Himself through Jesus Christ.
And if you have wandered away from Him, you do not have to keep hiding.
You do not have to manufacture a perfect testimony before returning.
Repentance is not pretending that sin was harmless.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who died and rose again.
Forgiveness is not God declaring that evil never mattered.
It is mercy made possible through the costly sacrifice of Christ.
And transformation is not a promise that your life will suddenly become painless.
It is the ongoing work of God's grace, reshaping your heart as you follow Jesus.
Perhaps you have been measuring your life by everything that has not happened.
The wedding that never came.
The child you never conceived.
The relationship that never healed.
The opportunity that never opened.
The years you wish you could recover.
But you are more than the things you are waiting for.
And you are more than the mistakes you cannot undo.
In Christ, a sinner can be forgiven.
A hardened heart can be humbled.
A wounded person can find hope.
A wandering believer can return.
A life marked by shame can become a testimony to grace.
Not because Jesus promises to erase every consequence of the past.
But because His mercy can give a repentant sinner a new future.
That is the Gospel.
And that is the message Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim.
Not a Christianity built around emotional excitement alone.
Not a faith that promises riches to everyone who gives.
Not a message that treats prayer as a machine for producing miracles.
But the truth of Scripture.
Jesus Christ crucified.
Jesus Christ risen.
Jesus Christ calling sinners to repentance and faith.
Jesus Christ restoring lives through grace.
You do not have to disclose private details.
You do not have to explain your pain to strangers.
But sometimes a small, honest confession reminds another struggling believer that they are not alone.
Not to make someone else's waiting feel smaller.
But to give glory to the One who sustained you.
Someone reading may be one difficult night away from giving up on prayer.
Your words might encourage them to keep turning toward Christ.
And perhaps you know someone who needs this message.
A wife carrying the grief of infertility.
A husband who does not know how to comfort her.
A friend whose prayers seem unanswered.
A parent grieving a loss.
A Christian who has begun confusing delayed blessings with divine rejection.
Not because every share guarantees that somebody will be saved.
Only the Gospel, through the work of God, brings salvation.
But because sharing biblical truth creates another opportunity for someone to encounter the message of Jesus.
One post may reach a person you have never met.
One testimony may open a conversation.
One Scripture may lead someone back to the Word of God.
And that is worth caring about.
Return to Genesis 25.
Read the actual passage.
Remember what Scripture says, and also what it does not say.
Then remember the greater story that leads to Christ.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is opened, Jesus is exalted, repentance is taken seriously, and wounded people are pointed toward the grace of God.

These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, deepen their understanding of the Gospel, strengthen their walk with Christ, and grow beyond momentary inspiration into lasting discipleship.
And there is another invitation I want to extend.
It is voluntary support for a ministry mission: helping us continue producing biblical encouragement, sharing discipleship resources, and reaching more people with the message of Jesus Christ.
For those who wish to give regularly, that support can be an expression of Christian generosity and stewardship.
But I want to be careful with something important.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, but from a willing heart.
You do not have to pay to glorify God.
It can help make continued writing, resource development, and broader Gospel outreach possible.
These items are simply an added expression of appreciation.
The deeper purpose is discipleship.
More Scripture.
More opportunities to learn.
More encouragement to pursue holiness.
More reminders that Jesus is sufficient.
More resources to help people understand the Word rather than merely react to a powerful quote.
And more opportunities to place Christ-centered teaching before people who may never walk through a church door.
Pray that we never exchange biblical truth for popularity.
Pray that we never confuse emotional reactions with genuine repentance.
Pray that every article points people beyond the writer and toward the Savior.
Pray that people who encounter Gospel Warrior will be encouraged to open their Bibles, seek a faithful local church, love their neighbors, and follow Jesus more closely.
Because that is what matters.
But helping people become disciples.
Not simply producing content that moves emotions.
But proclaiming truth that calls people to Christ.
Not simply collecting comments and shares.
But encouraging real faith, genuine repentance, and love that reaches beyond a screen.
And now, before you leave, come back with me to that ancient household.
Isaac was forty when he married Rebekah.
He was sixty when their twins were born.
Between those two verses lay twenty years.
Twenty years that the biblical narrator does not fill with elaborate descriptions.
Twenty years we cannot reconstruct in detail.
But twenty years that remind us how much human experience can exist inside the quiet spaces of Scripture.
Then came Esau.
Then Jacob.
Then generations of conflict and covenant history.
And eventually, in the line of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, came Jesus Christ.
The Savior who would bear the sins of His people.
The Savior who would die and rise again.
The Savior who still calls the weary, the guilty, the grieving, and the lost to come to Him.
Maybe the thing you have been praying for has not arrived.
Maybe it never will arrive in the form you hoped.
I will not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But I can point you to what He has revealed.
Jesus Christ is risen.
His Gospel is true.
His grace is sufficient for those who belong to Him.
And no season of waiting can make the cross meaningless or the empty tomb powerless.
So bring Him your grief.
Bring Him your unanswered questions.
Bring Him your repentance.
Bring Him the parts of your life you are ashamed to discuss.
And when you have no strength left to impress anyone, remember that the invitation of the Gospel was never to impress God with your strength.
It was to come to Jesus in faith.
The deepest miracle is not that Rebekah's empty womb was filled, but that through Jesus Christ, even a heart emptied by sin and despair can be brought from death into life.
